strengths: Identifies and analyzes an important failure mode in native text-to-3D generative models, termed the 'sink trap', where out-of-distribution text prompts lead to insensitive or poor geometric control.

Provides a simple and effective empirical strategy: performing Euler inversion and Null-Text Inversion with an empty source prompt stabilizes trajectories and improves reconstruction, supported by L1/LPIPS metrics and velocity-norm analysis.
Demonstrates text-driven 3D shape editing using only a native 3D generative model, without auxiliary 2D inpainting models, masks, or image-based priors, and shows multiview consistency qualitatively.
Includes useful comparisons to text-to-image inversion, prompt-type ablations, runtime comparison with VoxHammer, and detailed supplemental implementation notes and limitations.
Addresses an underexplored problem—inversion and editing in native 3D generative latent spaces—and the findings are likely to be of interest to the 3D generation/editing community.
weaknesses: The study relies on a single 3D backbone (TRELLIS, first-stage structure model). Claims about general 'native text-to-3D generative models' or broad 3D failure modes are not established across different models, datasets, or training regimes.

Methodological novelty is limited: the core approach is essentially applying existing Euler inversion and Null-Text Inversion with an empty prompt. The 'sink trap' is characterized informally rather than formally defined or rigorously detected.

The diversity ratio R and velocity-norm OOD analysis are heuristic and lack validation as reliable diagnostic tools. The language-diversity study uses only 8 subjects and no confidence intervals or formal statistical tests.

Editing evaluation is insufficient: SigLIP alignment with the edit prompt is reported, but there is no quantitative measure of source preservation, pose consistency, or geometric fidelity, and no user study. Baselines are weak or fail on a large fraction of cases, and stronger relevant 3D editing methods are not compared.

Some technical details are inconsistent or unclear, e.g., Algorithm 1's classifier-free guidance formulation appears reversed relative to standard CFG and the main text, and some table/figure references are erroneous. High variance in key metrics (e.g., L1 76.55 ± 73.35) weakens statistical conclusions.

The comparison with text-to-image inversion may not fully support the claim that 3D is uniquely sensitive to out-of-distribution prompts; in FLUX and Stable Diffusion, empty prompts also improve reconstruction, suggesting prompt-conditioned inversion can be suboptimal in image models as well.

The claim of 'first high-fidelity 3D editing driven solely by a target text prompt' is strong but not adequately substantiated given the limited baselines, small-scale evaluation, and lack of source-preservation metrics.

strengths: Identifies and empirically studies an important failure mode in native text-to-3D models: prompt insensitivity or 'sink trap', using diversity ratios and velocity-norm analysis.

Proposes a simple, training-free inversion strategy using an empty prompt with null-text optimization, and shows improved reconstruction of complex non-rigid DT4D shapes compared with approximate-prompt inversion.
Demonstrates text-driven geometric retargeting without auxiliary masks or 2D inpainting priors, with a fast 9s-per-edit pipeline and visually multiview-consistent results.
Provides implementation details, dataset preparation, prompt files, and qualitative editing examples; uses publicly available TRELLIS and DT4D resources.
Honestly lists limitations, including failure cases for geometrically out-of-distribution poses.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially Null-Text Inversion adapted to a 3D rectified-flow model with an empty prompt; there is no new inversion algorithm or formal theory explaining the sink-trap phenomenon.

The 'sink trap' is not rigorously defined or validated. The diversity analysis lacks details such as number of prompts per subject, generation variance, statistical significance, and controls showing that R<1 reflects model collapse rather than text-encoder behavior or sampling noise.

The inversion comparison is not well controlled: TRELLIS reconstruction uses L1 on coarse voxels, while image models use PSNR/LPIPS on pixels, so the cross-domain comparison is not directly meaningful. Empty prompts also improve FLUX/SD reconstructions in their own experiments, weakening the claim that this is a uniquely 3D failure mode.

Editing evaluation is weak: only SigLIP alignment scores are reported, with very low absolute values and no variance, and only two baselines are compared. There are no standard 3D editing baselines, no quantitative pose/structure preservation metrics, and no user study. VoxHammer's failure on DT4D may be due to dataset/adaptation choices rather than a fundamental limitation.

Several claims are overstated. The approach still requires an input 3D shape and inversion; it is not prompt-only editing. The title and framing conflate out-of-distribution text prompts with out-of-distribution 3D shapes, which are not clearly disentangled.

Missing ablations: no study of CFG scale, number of inversion/sampling steps, NTI inner steps, prompt choice, or the role of the second-stage model. It is unclear how the second-stage model is 'fixed and seeded' while edited textures still appear to change in the figures.

Writing and presentation issues remain: typos ('by simply by simply'), inconsistent table references ('Table 1., Supp. Mat'), undefined notation, and a confusing classifier-free guidance equation in the preliminaries.

Reproducibility is only partial: no code release is mentioned, several experimental protocols are underspecified, and the quantitative evidence does not convincingly support the high-fidelity editing claim given the acknowledged failure modes.

strengths: Identifies and analyzes a timely failure mode in native text-to-3D generative models: text-conditioned inversion can collapse into 'sink traps' where prompt changes barely affect geometry. The diversity-ratio and velocity-norm analyses provide useful empirical evidence for this phenomenon, and the comparison with T2I models helps contextualize it.

Proposes a simple but effective remedy: performing inversion with an empty/null prompt and stabilizing the trajectory via null-text optimization. This accesses the unconditional geometric prior and yields substantially better reconstruction of complex, non-rigid, out-of-distribution shapes in the reported experiments.

Demonstrates that unconditional inversion can still support text-driven editing without auxiliary 2D inpainting models, masks, or multiview image priors. The editing pipeline is also much faster than the VoxHammer baseline (reported 9s vs. 197s per edit).

The paper includes a reasonable empirical study with DT4D and TRELLIS-generated assets, quantitative metrics (L1, LPIPS, SigLIP), multiview consistency checks, and qualitative editing examples. The supplementary material provides implementation details and prompt files, supporting reproducibility.

The core insight, that the geometric expressivity of the 3D generative model exceeds its language-constrained controllability, is valuable for the community and could motivate further work on 3D inversion, OOD detection, and native 3D editing.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat limited: the proposed method is essentially NTI with an empty source prompt, and the 'sink trap' is mainly an empirical/prompt-space observation rather than a formal characterization of the model's latent dynamics. The contribution would be stronger with deeper analysis of why textual conditioning collapses in these regions.

Evaluation is restricted. The main editing comparisons use only TRELLIS and VoxHammer, where VoxHammer fails on a large fraction of DT4D cases and native TRELLIS editing mainly changes texture. The datasets are relatively small (80 TRELLIS shapes, 200 DT4D shapes), and the reported SigLIP improvement is modest without confidence intervals or significance analysis.

The algorithmic description of classifier-free guidance in Alg. 1 appears inconsistent with the standard CFG formula: it defines v_cond as the empty-prompt velocity and v_uncond as the optimized unconditional embedding, then uses v = v_cond + w(v_cond - v_uncond). This may be a naming issue or a sign error, but as written it is unclear and should be corrected/clarified.

The claim of being the first high-fidelity editing approach using only a native text-to-3D model and no additional input beyond the target prompt may be overstated: the method still requires a source 3D shape, its voxelization, and null-text optimization. It also does not completely eliminate editing failures, as the limitations section acknowledges for extreme OOD poses.

Some evidence for the central mismatch is mixed: several semantic categories in Table 1 have diversity ratios close to or above 1, and the supplementary results show that empty prompts can also improve inversion for image models such as Stable Diffusion. This does not invalidate the 3D-specific failure mode, but it weakens the strong framing of a uniquely 3D text-geometry mismatch.

Editing quality is evaluated mostly through prompt-alignment and qualitative examples; structural preservation of the source shape is not quantitatively measured, and there is no user study. This makes it harder to judge whether edits are consistently high-fidelity rather than visually cherry-picked.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and underexplored problem: inversion and text-driven editing directly in native text-to-3D generative models, rather than relying on 2D priors or masks.

It identifies an interesting behavioral failure mode, termed the 'sink trap', and provides qualitative and quantitative evidence that approximate/OOD prompts destabilize inversion in TRELLIS and other 3D models.
The proposed unconditional/empty-prompt inversion is simple, easy to implement, and consistently improves reconstruction across TRELLIS, LN3Diff, and GaussianAnything in the reported metrics.
The editing pipeline enables text-only semantic edits without masks or image-based priors, and the qualitative examples demonstrate nontrivial geometric retargeting and multiview consistency.
The paper is well organized, includes implementation details, dataset descriptions, prompts, and a limitations section, and reports a large efficiency advantage over optimization-heavy baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim that unconditional priors reveal the model's true geometric expressivity is not adequately supported. Inversion/reconstruction of a given shape does not show that the model's unconditional prior can produce that shape from random noise; NTI also optimizes per-shape null embeddings, so the method is not purely exploiting the unconditional distribution.

The diversity-ratio metric R is ad hoc and uncalibrated. It uses SigLIP embeddings rather than the generative model's own text encoder, and the cross-modal ratio R < 1 may simply reflect embedding-space variance rather than demonstrating a 'sink trap'. No direct correlation is shown between low R and inversion/editing failure.

The experimental evaluation is limited in scale and rigor. Reconstruction is mainly on a small DT4D subset and TRELLIS-generated samples, while editing uses only 30 rendered views per sample, no human study, and a VLM score from LLaVA-1.5-7B without confidence intervals or significance testing.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and potentially unfair. VoxHammer fails on a large fraction of DT4D samples but is still included, while relevant recent inversion-based 3D editing methods such as 3D-Latte are discussed but not compared.

The technical novelty is modest: the method is essentially Null-Text Inversion with an empty source prompt. The reconstruction results show Euler + empty prompt is already close to NTI + empty prompt, leaving the specific role of the proposed optimization unclear.

The claim that this is the first high-fidelity 3D editing pipeline using only a target prompt is overstated, since the method still requires the source mesh, a successful inversion, and optional per-shape null-text optimization, and it fails on some OOD poses as shown in the limitations.

strengths: Identifies an interesting failure mode in native text-to-3D generative models: the proposed 'sink trap' where prompt changes fail to alter geometry despite the model retaining geometric expressivity.
Provides a simple and computationally efficient inversion/editing pipeline that avoids 2D image priors and auxiliary inpainting models; edits average around 9 seconds per edit in the reported setup.
Evaluates the core reconstruction finding across multiple 3D generative models (TRELLIS, LN3Diff, GaussianAnything) and includes image-domain comparisons with Stable Diffusion and FLUX.
Includes qualitative editing results, multiview consistency visualizations, and a limitations section that openly notes failure cases for geometrically out-of-distribution poses.

The paper raises a useful question about how text conditioning can be misaligned with geometric expressivity in 3D generative models, which may inspire follow-up work on better conditioning or OOD detection.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is limited: the method is essentially standard null-text inversion using an empty source prompt. The paper does not introduce a new algorithm, a formal characterization of the 'sink trap', or a principled solution to OOD text guidance; it mainly avoids text conditioning during inversion.

The main claim 'first high-fidelity 3D editing using only a native text-to-3D model and without any additional input beyond the target prompt' is overstated. The pipeline requires an input source mesh, voxelization, VAE encoding, inversion, and NTI optimization, and editing still depends on text prompts and optimized unconditional embeddings.

The 'sink trap' analysis is not rigorous. The diversity ratio R = Δvis/Δtxt uses SigLIP cosine distances over a small set of subjects and generated prompts, with no statistical testing; values near 1 or above actually contradict the claimed collapse, and the metric can be confounded by prompt generation, encoder behavior, and sampling variance.

The velocity-norm analysis is weak and largely expected: approximate prompts with classifier-free guidance naturally produce larger guidance terms, but this does not establish that the trajectory is entering a low-density region or that the model is in a 'sink trap'.

The editing evaluation is insufficient. It reports only prompt-alignment metrics (SigLIP, CLIP, LLaVA-based VLM score) and does not quantify preservation of source shape identity, pose, or structure. No user study or standard 3D editing metric is provided.

The baseline comparison is concerning. VoxHammer reportedly fails on 67% of DT4D samples, yet it is still used in a quantitative table without clarifying how failures are handled. Important related latent-space 3D editing methods such as 3D-LATTE are not directly compared, and the NTI + approximate-prompt editing baseline is absent from the main comparison.

Method details are unclear and sometimes confusing. The roles of conditional vs. unconditional embeddings are inconsistently described, the editing formula using the optimized unconditional embedding is not fully specified, and the influence/role of the second-stage TRELLIS model in editing is ambiguous.

The qualitative claims are supported mainly by selected visual examples, with no failure rates or robustness statistics. The datasets are small (200 DT4D shapes, 80 TRELLIS-generated shapes), and the number of edits evaluated quantitatively is limited.

Writing and citation quality need improvement. There are citation errors (e.g., Vox-E is cited as [47] in Table 3, which corresponds to a different paper), typos, and awkward phrasing throughout, which hinders reproducibility and clarity.

The paper does not actually solve OOD text-conditioned editing: failures remain for out-of-distribution edit prompts or rare poses, and the proposed method simply bypasses OOD text during inversion. This sharply limits the claimed generality of the approach.

strengths: Identifies and characterizes a real and important failure mode ('sink trap') in native text-to-3D generative models, supported by quantitative diversity ratios across categories and models.
Provides useful trajectory-level analysis (velocity norm instability under OOD prompts) and contrasts 3D inversion with 2D image inversion, giving insight into why text conditioning collapses.

Proposes a simple but effective unconditional inversion strategy (empty prompt + null-text optimization) that decouples geometric expressivity from linguistic conditioning and yields high-fidelity reconstruction of complex shapes.
Demonstrates text-driven 3D editing using only a native text-to-3D model, without external 2D priors or masks, with strong quantitative gains over baselines and efficient runtime.
Paper is clearly written, well-organized, and candid about limitations; additional experiments and qualitative results support the claims.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively simple: using an empty prompt for inversion plus existing null-text optimization; the novelty lies mainly in the analysis and application rather than a substantially new algorithm.

The analysis is largely empirical/heuristic; diversity ratio R and velocity norm are useful diagnostics but no formal characterization or proof is provided for the sink-trap phenomenon or why unconditional inversion avoids it.

Evaluation is limited mainly to TRELLIS for editing, with only partial generalization tests on other native 3D models (LN3Diff, GaussianAnything) for inversion quality, not editing; the dataset size (200 DT4D + 80 generated shapes) is also modest.

Editing metrics rely on CLIP/SigLIP and a 1-5 VLM rating, which may not fully capture 3D structural fidelity, pose preservation, or semantic correctness; stronger human evaluation or geometric metrics would improve confidence.
Comparison with VoxHammer is uneven because it fails on 67% of DT4D samples; while this supports the paper's point about inversion instability, it complicates fair quantitative comparison.
Some extreme out-of-distribution poses still fail, and the method inherits limitations of the underlying generative model; robustness and failure detection remain open.
